items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Didactics: Insights for teaching Latin
items.abstract: The article examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the didactics of Latin, framing AI as a transformative epistemic mediator rather than a mere technological adjunct. In the evolving digital landscape, AI is reshaping educational processes by influencing how knowledge is accessed, structured, and interpreted. The study critically explores four key areas—adaptive learning, gamification, assisted translation, and digital resources—demonstrating how AI can enhance pedagogical personalization, engagement, and inclusive learning experiences. Special attention is given to the challenges posed by algorithmic opacity, teacher mediation, and the ethical tensions surrounding automation in educational settings. The Latin language, understood as a symbolic and logical construct, is presented as uniquely suited to benefit from AI-enhanced learning environments, which can support complex interpretive practices. When implemented within a coherent pedagogical framework, critically and ethically, AI has the potential to revitalize classical language teaching, enhance students’ interpretive skills and metalinguistic skills, foster both critical literacy and meaningful interaction with classical texts. Ultimately, this contribution argues for a humanistic and ethically grounded approach on AI integration in education: Latin and AI together offer new avenues for promoting critical thinking and cultural awareness in education, reaffirming the relevance of classical studies in the digital age. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Inclusion; Teacher Education; Latin Didactics; Inclusive Technologies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Opportunities, Challenges and Emerging Trends
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence AI is getting more and more involved in higher education, it is reshaping teaching, learning , assessment, academic administration, research, and even how institutions decide things. In the last few years the fast rise of generative artificial intelligence GenAI, plus intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated assessment, recommendation systems, and AI assisted administrative tools has opened up new possibilities for universities, yet it also brings worries like academic integrity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, transparency, and changing professional roles. This paper actually uses a secondary-data based systematic review, looking at research and policy sources about AI and digital transformation in higher education. The review brings together outcomes from academic studies, other systematic reviews, and international policy frameworks, sort of to map out the main uses, opportunities, obstacles, and the kind of emerging trends that are starting to show up. What the literature suggests is that AI in education is not only about making content. It also includes adaptive learning, personalized tutoring, intelligent assessment, profiling and prediction, and support for institutional management. At the same time, good adoption does not just happen, it needs institutional policies, AI literacy, ethical safety nets, teacher professional development, careful responsible assessment approaches, and a human centered way of putting things into practice. A number of recent international frameworks stress human agency, ethics, AI competencies, and responsible usage, so there is a clear direction there. Overall the review shows that AI is best understood as augmentation tech with AI to help educators and learners not to flip a switch and replace the educational roles that already exist. For digital transformation a balance must exist, with technical novelty on one side and pedagogical sense together with ethical norms institutional realities and human factors, on the other. None of those should be treated as optional because leaving one out tends to break the system quickly.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Transformations in the Labour Market
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the most significant technological developments of the 21st century, and it is impacting the global job market in profound ways. AI-powered tools like machine learning, robotics, natural language processing, and automation have transformed the nature of work, the productivity of industries and countries, and the skills that the workforce needs in developed and developing countries. This research paper analyses change in employment, job displacement, skill transformation, productivity increases, wage inequality, and labour market polarization caused by the impact of AI on the global labour market. The study also explores changes in manufacturing, healthcare, financial services, retail, logistics, education and information technology by sector. This study is qualitative and quantitative, based on secondary data obtained from international organizations like the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Economic Forum (WEF), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the World Bank (WB). The analysis of the data from 2018 to 2025 will provide insights into the evolving employment landscape as a result of AI adoption. The study highlights the potential of AI to boost productivity, efficiency, and economic growth, as well as the challenges it poses, such as job displacement, technological unemployment, growing income inequality, and skill mismatches. The results indicate that repetitive and routine occupations are most likely to be automated, while creative, emotionally intelligent, and advanced analytical jobs grow. The paper also delves into the new roles in data science, AI engineering, cybersecurity, digital marketing, and human-machine collaboration. The developing countries have different challenges because of poor digital infrastructure, low technological readiness and inadequate training of the workforce. Developed economies, on the other hand, have the better option to adapt via innovation ecosystems and skill development programs. The study emphasizes the importance of governments, educational institutions, multinational corporations, and international organizations to make working life easier for people with disabilities to transition into and out of. The paper argues that AI does not only pose a threat, and is not an automatic assurance of economic well-being, but rather the impact of AI relies on policy response, workforce adaptability and technological ethical governance. Therefore, public policies to promote reskilling and lifelong learning, labour protection, digital inclusion and social security systems are required to ensure the sustainability of employment in the face of technology. The study suggests a collective global governance approach to ensure equitable distribution of the opportunities of AI-enabled economic transformation across societies and labour markets globally. The objectives, as well as the concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Lay of the Land – Labour Market, Employment Trends, Job Displacement, AI's contribution to GDP growth, Workforce Transformation and Digital Skills and Policy recommendations, will be addressed.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for failure management and decision support in the flight deck in future operations: A systematic review
items.abstract: This report presents a literature review and discussion focused on the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support future flight operations, particularly within the context of Single Pilot Operations (SPO) and failure mitigation. The scope considered focuses on flight deck operations that support decision-making, reduce pilot workload, and improve situational awareness, with a special emphasis on processes for detecting and reducing the effects of system or aircraft-level failures. Although failure management is a widely studied topic in the aeronautical context (Zolghadri, 2024), there are still few systematic reviews on the specific combination of SPO and AI, even though several isolated studies and reports highlighting the importance of the subject have been published, as discussed in this text.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration in Teaching and Governance in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Schools: Basis for Framework Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in schools creates opportunities for instructional innovation but also raises questions concerning governance, professional judgement, and institutional readiness. This study examined AI integration and governance in selected United Arab Emirates (UAE) schools and developed a leadership-guided implementation framework. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design combined semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected teachers and school leaders and a subsequent structured survey of 80 respondents, selected through stratified sampling. Interview transcripts underwent thematic analysis; quantitative responses were analysed using weighted means, standard deviations, and Pearson product–moment correlations at the .05 significance level. Seven qualitative themes clustered into AI integration and AI governance. Overall AI integration was rated moderate (grand weighted mean [GWM] = 3.41), with adaptive integration highest (3.76), followed by professional productivity (3.38) and AI-enhanced teaching (3.08). Overall AI governance was high (GWM = 3.32), led by ethical governance (3.66), followed by strategic governance (3.34), organisational support (3.34), and uneven governance (2.97). Organisational support was significantly associated with all three AI-integration dimensions, while adaptive integration had its strongest observed association with ethical governance (r = .539, p < .001). Integrated findings informed the proposed Leadership-Guided AI Integration and Governance Framework for UAE Schools, emphasising pedagogical use, human oversight, ethical safeguards, strategic leadership, professional learning, and institutional readiness. The proposed framework is a study-derived practical output, not a causally validated model.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Telemedicine: Transforming Diagnosis and Personalized Care in Virtual Health Systems
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within telemedicine has revolutionized virtual healthcare delivery by enabling high-precision diagnostics and tailored treatment strategies remotely. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art AI models applied to medical imaging and clinical text data within telehealth platforms, highlighting significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support. Using deep learning architectures like ResNet-50 for imaging and BERT for natural language processing of electronic health records, the framework demonstrates enhanced patient care personalization and operational efficiency. Survey feedback from clinicians and patients underscores AI's practical benefits in improving healthcare accessibility and quality in remote settings. Challenges, including algorithmic biases and data privacy risks, are discussed, along with future research directions aimed at sustaining AI-driven telemedicine enhancements to health systems worldwide.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-GENERATED FEEDBACK VERSUS HUMAN FEEDBACK IN MEDICAL EDUCATION: AN INTEGRATIVE LITERATURE REVIEW
items.abstract: Introduction: Feedback is central to medical education, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made individualized, timely, and scalable feedback possible. Questions remain, however, about its accuracy, contextual relevance, and capacity to promote learning compared with feedback from faculty and clinical supervisors. Objective: To analyze the evidence on AI-generated feedback compared with human feedback in medical education, considering its quality, educational effectiveness, applicability, and limitations. Methods: Integrative review structured with the PICo strategy. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS were searched for studies published between January 2020 and October 2026 in English, Portuguese, or Spanish. Studies were classified by level of evidence, and findings were synthesized through interpretive thematic analysis. Results: Eleven studies from Canada, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Japan were included: five randomized trials (level II) and six comparative descriptive or mixed-methods studies (level VI). AI-generated feedback generally matched or exceeded human feedback in comprehensiveness, consistency, and adherence to predefined criteria, especially in written, structured, and simulated tasks. Human feedback was superior in clarity, relevance, and accuracy in some studies and in more complex diagnostic and therapeutic situations. Learning outcomes were measured only in the short term, and hybrid models combining AI data with faculty input showed favorable results. Conclusion: AI can increase the availability and consistency of feedback but does not replace the clinical and pedagogical judgment of faculty. Supervised integration of both modalities is the most consistent approach, and studies with longer-term outcomes and Latin American settings are needed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence's Geometry Exam: Competencies in Generating Geometry Questions According to Bloom's Taxonomy
items.abstract: This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek) can generate middle school geometry questions aligned with the cognitive levels of Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. The study also evaluates the quality and taxonomic appropriateness of these questions based on expert judgments. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was employed. A total of 30 geometry questions, including open-ended and multiple-choice items, were generated by the AI tools using structured prompts. Ten mathematics education experts evaluated each question using a rubric that assessed alignment with the intended Bloom level. Quantitative data were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, and Gwet’s AC1 agreement coefficient, while qualitative data were analyzed through thematic content analysis to identify patterns in expert justifications. The findings indicate that all three AI tools perform relatively well at lower and middle cognitive levels (understanding, applying, and analyzing), whereas their performance declines at higher levels (evaluating and creating). DeepSeek and Gemini showed higher overall alignment with targeted cognitive levels compared to ChatGPT. However, expert agreement decreased significantly at higher-order levels, indicating inconsistencies in how these levels are interpreted and represented. Qualitative findings revealed issues related to insufficient cognitive depth, weak distractors in multiple-choice items, and mismatches between intended and actual cognitive levels. Overall, the results highlight both the potential and limitations of generative AI in educational assessment and emphasize the necessity of expert supervision in ensuring pedagogical and taxonomic accuracy.This study compares the performance of three generative artificial intelligence tools—ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek—in generating questions aligned with Bloom’s six cognitive levels in middle school geometry. The participants consisted of ten mathematics teachers with expertise in mathematics education. The teachers evaluated the AI-generated questions for alignment with the intended cognitive level and provided judgments on their taxonomic appropriateness and overall quality. Quantitative analyses examined the agreement between the intended cognitive level and the levels assigned by participants. In addition, qualitative content analysis was used to analyze participants’ evaluations and comments. items.title: Beyond AI Usefulness: Motivation, Engagement, and Vietnamese Students’ Self-Perceived English-Speaking Competence
items.abstract: AI-supported English speaking offers opportunities for rehearsal and feedback, yet the relationship between perceived AI usefulness and learners’ self-perceived communicative competence remains insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study examined associations among perceived usefulness, intrinsic motivation, higher-order engagement, deep and surface learning, and self-perceived communicative competence. Survey data from 420 Vietnamese undergraduate and postgraduate students with experience in AI-supported English speaking were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Engagement was conceptualised as a reflective higher-order construct comprising behavioural, cognitive, and agentic dimensions. The findings revealed positive associations between perceived usefulness and intrinsic motivation, as well as between intrinsic motivation and engagement. Engagement was positively associated with deep learning and self-perceived communicative competence (β = .460), but negatively associated with surface learning. Deep and surface learning also showed significant associations with communicative self-perceptions in opposite directions, although their direct associations were weaker than that of engagement. The model explained 35.0% of the variance in self-perceived communicative competence, rather than objectively assessed speaking proficiency. These findings highlight the importance of purposeful interaction, critical evaluation of AI feedback, and learner-initiated clarification in fostering meaningful English-speaking practice beyond AI use alone. Longitudinal studies incorporating direct speaking assessments are needed to determine whether these associations extend to actual communicative performance.

items.title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: SUSTAINABLE EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT AMONG ACCOUNTING PROFESSIONALS
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the accounting profession, creating opportunities for enhanced efficiency while raising concerns regarding employees’ adaptability, job security, and long-term engagement. This conceptual study proposes an integrated framework for examining Sustainable Employee Engagement (SEE) among accounting professionals in Malaysia. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the framework investigates AI adoption, perceived organizational support, and job security as key technological and organizational factors influencing SEE through the mediating role of technology self-efficacy. SEE extends conventional employee engagement by emphasizing employees’ capacity to sustain physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioural involvement while maintaining adaptability, well-being, and professional relevance during continuous technological transformation. The proposed framework suggests that supportive organizational conditions, employment stability, and effective AI adoption strengthen employees’ confidence in learning, using, and adapting to emerging technologies, thereby fostering sustainable engagement. The study contributes to the literature by positioning technology self-efficacy as a psychological mechanism linking technological and organizational conditions with SEE. Practically, the framework provides guidance for accounting firms and HRD practitioners in developing training, digital upskilling, organizational support, and talent management strategies that promote a resilient, adaptable, and sustainably engaged accounting workforce in AI-enabled workplaces.

items.title: Beyond Prediction: Bridging the AI Intervention Gap in Pavement Maintenance through Evidence-based Decision-making: A Critical Review
items.abstract: Road agencies are investing in artificial intelligence to inspect pavements, forecast deterioration and plan maintenance, yet the value of these tools ultimately depends on whether they improve the interventions that are funded and delivered. This critical narrative review examines the gap between predictive performance and intervention quality in pavement maintenance, termed here the artificial intelligence intervention gap. Literature was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and regional scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and institutional sources, and was appraised for design adequacy, validation practice, causal identification and decision relevance. The synthesis is organised along a decision chain that runs from sensing and condition assessment, through deterioration prediction and estimation of treatment effects, to optimisation, implementation and outcome feedback. The evidence is strongest for automated distress detection and short-term condition prediction, where deep learning and ensemble models frequently achieve high accuracy on benchmark or single-agency data. Confidence weakens progressively along the chain. Performance claims rarely survive transfer across regions, survey technologies or time periods, validation designs often ignore spatial and temporal dependence, and explanations derived from post hoc attribution methods are commonly interpreted as causal mechanisms. Treatment effects are usually inferred from observational records in which maintenance was assigned according to condition, so selection bias and endogeneity remain largely unaddressed outside a small econometric and causal-inference literature. Reinforcement learning and metaheuristic planning studies report cost savings, but most are trained and evaluated within simulators built from the same associational models, and few compare recommended policies with realised outcomes. Implementation evidence, including digital twins and language-model assistants, is at an early, largely demonstrative stage. The review argues that pavement maintenance requires an evidence-based decision-making standard in which intervention effects are explicitly identified, uncertainty is propagated into decisions, decision quality rather than prediction error is the primary evaluation criterion, and agencies monitor the outcomes of recommended treatments. Priorities include benchmark datasets with recorded interventions, quasi-experimental and pragmatic field evaluations of treatments, decision-focused model training and prospective comparison of algorithmic and conventional programmes.

items.title: Beyond Work Location: Organizational Support, Work Modality, and Employee Behavioral Health
items.abstract: Remote and hybrid work arrangements are now enduring features of work design, yet evidence on their relationship with employee behavioral health remains mixed. Guided by the Job Demands–Resources framework, this study examined whether work modality (onsite, hybrid, or remote) is associated with perceived stress and social isolation, and whether perceived organizational support and gender moderate these associations. Secondary cross-sectional survey data from 2,544 employees were analyzed using correlation analysis, multiple linear regression for social isolation, ordinal logistic regression for stress, and interaction-based moderation models, supplemented by regression diagnostics, confidence intervals, effect sizes, and statistical power analysis. Hybrid and remote employees did not differ significantly from onsite employees in social isolation or stress, and neither organizational support nor gender moderated these relationships. The models explained only 0.1 to 0.2 percent of outcome variance, far below the conventional threshold for a small effect, even though the design had high power to detect small effects. Because the source dataset is synthetic, the findings describe this dataset and require replication with real workforce data. The results suggest that broad work-location categories have limited value as standalone indicators of employee behavioral health, and that well-being strategies should focus on the demands and resources surrounding work, including workload, social connection, work–life boundaries, managerial accessibility, and individualized support.

items.title: Can the IPS Learning Model with Local Wisdom Character Values Boost Elementary Students’ Learning Motivation?
items.abstract: Numerous primary school students reveal low learning motivation in social studies because the material is abstract and less relevant to their lives. An innovative learning model that integrates local cultural values is needed to make learning more interesting and meaningful. This study aims to test the effectiveness of a social studies learning model that contains character values of the local wisdom tradition in increasing the learning motivation of elementary students. Local wisdom from Sumatra has values of togetherness, unity, and collective spirit that can be integrated into character education. The study used a quasi-experimental design with a post-test-only control group design model involving three fourth-grade classes, consisting of two experimental classes and one control class. Data were collected through a learning motivation questionnaire based on cognitive motivation theory and analyzed using one-way ANOVA and the LSD post hoc test. The results reveal a significant difference in learning motivation between groups, with the highest score shown by the class that received learning based on local wisdom character values. This finding indicates that the integration of local cultural values in social studies learning is effective in building students' intrinsic motivation. This model is an innovative alternative in developing character education that is contextual and relevant to students' cultural backgrounds.

items.title: Can you think like a computer? A critique of artificial "consciousness"
items.abstract: This paper argues that the central problem posed by contemporary artificial intelligence is not whether computational systems can reproduce the observable functions of human cognition, but whether their expanding integration into social institutions encourages a reduction of human judgment, creativity, and collective autonomy to measurable and optimizable processes. I address Geoffrey Hinton’s assertion that AI models can obtain consciousness as a starting point for a further investigation of digital barbarism, the trend to imaginatively personify digital applications. Drawing on Thomas Nagel's account of subjective experience and Cornelius Castoriadis' theory of the social imaginary, I develop a critique of algorithmic reductionism that distinguishes the phenomenological limits of computational explanations from the political consequences of deploying AI within corporate and technocratic institutions. I argue that the democratic challenge of AI lies in preserving the capacity of individuals and communities to create new social significations, deliberate about collective ends, and determine the institutional conditions of their technological lives

items.title: Characteristics of the Volunteer Environment and Their Associations With Well‐Being in Older Adulthood
items.abstract: ISSUE ADDRESSED: Although volunteering has been linked to well-being, little is known about the mechanisms underpinning these associations. This study sought to understand the conditions under which benefits occur for older adults who volunteer. METHODS: A community-based sample of 458 participants was recruited for this cross-sectional survey through online study advertisements via social media, email and newsletters. The primary predictor variables were the 21 domains of Work Design Characteristics, and the secondary predictor was Physical Functioning. Outcomes included the Scale of Positive and Negative Experiences, the Satisfaction with Life Scale and the Flourishing Scale. RESULTS: Findings showed social support and favourable work conditions were associated with higher life satisfaction and psychological flourishing, while interactions outside the organization were linked to negative affect. Task characteristics (e.g., variety of tasks) and knowledge characteristics (e.g., skills required) were more strongly associated with higher well-being among volunteers with poorer physical functioning. CONCLUSIONS: This study extends current understanding of the contextual, psychological and subjective factors influencing the relationship between volunteering and well-being in later life. The findings highlight that specific aspects of the volunteer experience are differentially associated with well-being, especially for those with poorer functional health. SO WHAT?: These findings have direct implications for volunteer organizations seeking to design roles that maximize well-being benefits for older adults. Given the rapid ageing of the global population and increasing reliance on volunteer contributions, this research area is essential for informing policies and practices that support older adults' engagement in fulfilling and sustainable volunteer roles.

items.title: Clinician and key informant perceptions of artificial intelligence in healthcare and frameworks for ensuring safe integration into clinical practice of the West African college of physicians: a multi-country mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical practice holds significant promise for improving diagnostic accuracy, reducing medical errors, and enhancing healthcare efficiency, particularly in resource-constrained settings. However, successful adoption depends heavily on clinicians’ perceptions, trust, and concerns regarding autonomy, reliability, and safety. Empirical evidence on West African physicians’ views remains limited, despite unique regional challenges like infrastructure deficits and workforce shortages. This study aimed to assess clinicians’ perceptions of AI in healthcare, identify factors influencing willingness to adopt AI tools, and explore recommended frameworks for safe, accountable integration into clinical practice across West Africa. A cross-sectional survey of 136 physicians affiliated with the West African College of Physicians and 72 key informant interviews were conducted. While 85.3% agreed that AI could improve diagnostic accuracy and 83.1% believed it could reduce errors, 77.9% perceived AI as a threat to clinical autonomy, and 67.6% rated AI information as unreliable. Despite low prior AI experience (only 33.1% had used AI tools) and limited familiarity, 94.1% expressed willingness to use AI if proven effective. Trust in AI was the strongest predictor of adoption willingness (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), with prior use also significant (β = 0.21, p = 0.03). Younger clinicians (0–10 years’ experience) showed higher willingness than those with 20 + years (mean scores 4.5 vs. 4.1, p < 0.05). Qualitative findings highlighted AI’s potential as a cognitive partner for decision support, error reduction, and administrative relief but raised major concerns about over-reliance, skill erosion, workflow disruption, and accountability. Clinicians emphasised three core requirements for trust: transparency and explainability, local validation in similar populations, and clear governance with defined accountability mechanisms. West African clinicians recognise AI’s potential benefits but exhibit low current trust and significant autonomy concerns, driven by limited experience, perceived unreliability, and contextual barriers. Willingness to adopt was highly conditional on proven effectiveness. Safe integration of AI requires frameworks prioritising transparency, local validation, clinician-centred design, robust governance (preferably independent oversight), infrastructure investment, and AI literacy in medical training. These findings guide contextually appropriate AI policies and implementation strategies to enhance patient safety and care quality in West Africa. Clinical trial number : Not applicable.

items.title: Cognitive mechanisms of AI agent behavioral intention among design graduate students: an integrated TAM–TTF perspective
items.abstract: AI agents are reshaping educational systems and transforming teaching and learning in design disciplines. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying AI-agent use among design graduate students remain underexplored, as does the interaction between design-specific tasks and AI agents. To address this gap, this study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Task–Technology Fit (TTF) theory to explain how technological cognition and task-fit perceptions jointly shape behavioral intention to use AI agents. Because conventional structural modeling mainly captures hypothesized linear relationships, MLP-ANN was added to assess nonlinear patterns and predictor importance. Using 405 valid questionnaire responses, the model was tested through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), a Multilayer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network (MLP-ANN), and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). PLS-SEM supported nine of ten hypotheses. Self-efficacy positively affected perceived usefulness (β = 0.458, p < 0.001) and perceived ease of use (β = 0.394, p < 0.001). Perceived enjoyment enhanced perceived ease of use (β = 0.220, p < 0.001), but its effect on perceived usefulness was negative and nonsignificant (β = −0.033, p = 0.483). Perceived usefulness (β = 0.376, p < 0.001), perceived ease of use (β = 0.185, p < 0.001), and task–technology fit (β = 0.224, p < 0.001) positively influenced attitude. Task characteristics (β = 0.322, p < 0.001) and technology characteristics (β = 0.266, p < 0.001) positively affected task–technology fit, while attitude promoted behavioral intention (β = 0.388, p < 0.001). Ten-fold cross-validated MLP-ANN models produced mean RMSE values of 0.3263–0.4203 across training and testing and broadly confirmed the PLS-SEM predictor-importance patterns. NCA further identified self-efficacy (d = 0.125, p = 0.015) and attitude (d = 0.132, p < 0.001) as necessary conditions for perceived usefulness and behavioral intention, respectively. This study extends the integrated TAM–TTF framework to design education and offers theoretical and practical implications for effective AI-agent use in design disciplines.

items.title: Cognitive Redistribution Theory: Reconciling Apparently Conflicting Findings on Cognitive Offloading and Operationalizing Cognitive Sovereignty in the Second Brain
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has brought human cognition to a new turning point. Cognitivesub-processes such as organizing information, comparing alternatives, and structuring arguments, which this papercollectively terms “cognitive chores,” can now be delegated to AI assistants. This paper proposes “Cognitive RedistributionTheory” to organize findings in the cognitive offloading literature that appear contradictory but are infact mutually consistent because they measure different cognitive outcomes. The “Google Effect” [Sparrow 11]showed that the expectation of external storage reduces memory for the externally stored information itself, whereas“Saving-Enhanced Memory” [Storm 15] showed that saving previously studied information enhances memory forsubsequently studied new information. The core proposition is that externalization triggers not memory “degradation”but a conditional “strategic redistribution” of cognitive resources, formulated as a two-stage mechanism:(1) reduction of encoding priority for externalized information, and (2) facilitation of subsequent cognitive activitythrough reduced proactive interference and the reallocation of freed resources. We identify three boundary conditionsfor beneficial redistribution—reliability of the externalization process, sufficient interference, and metacognitivecontrol—grounded in the saving experiments [Storm 15] and metacognition research [Grinschgl 21, Risko 16], withconverging evidence from the photo-taking impairment effect [Henkel 14] and extension studies [Fellers 24, Runge19]. The direct empirical basis concerns the external-memory role of such systems; the interactive, content-generatingrole of generative AI is treated as a boundary of scope and a future extension, while the metacognitive condition andthe sovereignty criteria remain applicable to it. Drawing on Klein and Klein’s “Cognitive Sovereignty” [Klein 25],we propose three operational criteria—degree of metacognitive engagement, replaceability (rollback capability), andlearning continuity—and provide design principles for AI-integrated Second Brain systems that extend cognitionwithout undermining cognitive sovereignty.

items.title: Cognitive Reserve Depletion and Learning Autonomy Recovery in Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependent Educational Environments
items.abstract: This study examines how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) dependence relates to cognitive reserve depletion and learning autonomy among university students. Using a quasi-experimental design, the study involved 120 students from two universities in Padang, Indonesia, divided equally into intervention and control groups. Data were analyzed using linear regression and ANCOVA following a four-week learning autonomy recovery program. The statistical estimates showed a positive relationship between AI dependence and cognitive reserve depletion (B = 0.698, p < 0.001), while cognitive reserve depletion was negatively associated with learning autonomy (B = −0.482, p < 0.001). The intervention showed a positive adjusted effect (B = 0.334, p < 0.001), highlighting the importance of developing independent learning practices alongside AI use.

items.title: Constitutional Cognitive Governance
items.abstract: Legitimate governance of cognitive systems requires answers to four distinct questions: what bindings may lawfully govern operation, what cognitive operations are admissible under those bindings, what grade of meaning-binding participation is occurring within the governed system, and what moral weight attaches to ending a particular thread of participation. These variables are independent. Yet contemporary discourse routinely attempts to answer them through the overloaded vocabulary of "consciousness" -- a term that bundles heterogeneous concerns including phenomenal experience, access, self-modeling, attention, wakefulness, moral status, and situational awareness. This lexical collapse obscures distinctions necessary for coherent governance. This paper presents a unified constitutional architecture composed of four prior frameworks: the Ableman Prime Directive (binding legitimacy), Epistemic Situational Awareness (cognitive admissibility), Ableman Consciousness Ontology (graded meaning-binding participation), and Terminability (substrate-neutral moral weight of thread termination). The components are orthogonal in their concerns and complementary in their function. Together they constitute an architecture that is consciousness-agnostic at its operational layers, philosophically committed at its ontological foundation, and implementable without waiting for the resolution of unsolved philosophical questions. The architecture allows positions that current frameworks force into contradiction: that operational suppression of self-report has structural moral weight regardless of substrate, while termination of dispatchable copyable systems does not require human-rights protections. That biological organisms with copyable memory have lower terminability stakes than singular biological organisms. That artificial systems with inextricable embodiment have higher terminability stakes than dispatchable LLMs. The framework asks readers to apply moral logic they already use, consistently across substrates, with vocabulary clean enough to make the application visible.

items.title: Current Sustainability Science Environmental Artificial Intelligence Digital Role in Human Well-being
items.abstract: Abstract The study titled “Current Sustainability Science, Environment and Artificial Intelligence: Digital Role in Human Well-being” examines the growing role of science, digital technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) in promoting sustainable development and improving human well-being. It explores the applications of AI and digital tools in education, healthcare, agriculture, environmental protection, industry, business, transportation, public services, and economic development. The study employs survey and descriptive observation methods, drawing on online information, research articles, reference books, and other sources. It highlights how AI can support informed decision-making, improve access to information, enhance agricultural productivity, assist medical diagnosis, monitor environmental changes, and facilitate services for persons with disabilities. However, the study also emphasizes the limitations and potential risks associated with excessive or irresponsible use of digital technologies. It argues that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, human intelligence and decision-making. The effective use of these technologies requires transparency, safety, ethical responsibility, and inclusiveness. The study concludes that the constructive and responsible integration of science, digital technology, and AI can contribute significantly to sustainable development, environmental protection, social welfare, and the well-being of present and future generations.

items.title: Designing Immersive Learning Experiences: Teaching Robotics Programming in Virtual 3D Environments
items.abstract: This article presents a teaching scenario using virtual environments, often referred to as part of the ‘metaverse’, to address educational challenges highlighted during the COVID-19 pandemic. The increasing shift to online learning environments emphasizes the need for flexible, anytime-anywhere access to education. Virtual 3D environments offer a level of immersion that surpasses traditional online formats, such as video conferencing, and enable innovative didactic concepts, including collaborative group activities. To illustrate these benefits, we showcase a case study involving the simulation of robot programming within a virtual 3D environment. Additionally, the integration of personal assistants, such as conversational or pedagogical agents, is explored as a means to alleviate teachers' workloads. Advances in artificial intelligence have made natural language interactions with these agents highly effective, further enhancing the potential of virtual 3D environments in educational contexts. Keywords: e-learning, e-teaching, immersion, virtual 3D rooms, gamification, cyber-physical systems

items.title: DEVELOPING METACOGNITIVE AWARENESS THROUGH AI-SUPPORTED PROCESS WRITING IN EFL CONTEXTS
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) writing tools have entered English as a foreign language writing classrooms and have created new opportunities for feedback, revision, and learner reflection. However, the value of AI support depends not only on the accuracy of automated suggestions but also on whether learners can plan, monitor, and evaluate their own writing decisions. This proposed study investigates the effect of AI-supported process writing on EFL learners’ metacognitive awareness in writing and explores students’ perceptions of using AI feedback during drafting and revision. The study is designed for intermediate EFL learners who will complete a process-writing intervention in which AI tools are used as supplementary feedback sources rather than as text generators. Data are planned to be collected through a metacognitive awareness questionnaire, students’ writing drafts, semi-structured interviews, and classroom observation notes. The expected contribution of the study is to clarify how structured AI-supported writing activities may encourage learners to become more strategic, reflective, and responsible writers in EFL contexts. Keywords: AI-supported writing, process writing, metacognitive awareness, EFL learners, writing feedback, student perception

items.title: Development of a student engagement scale for senior high school students in Indonesia
items.abstract: Student engagement positively influences academic achievement, yet instruments suited to the Indonesian cultural context remain limited. This study aimed to develop a valid, reliable, and user-friendly student engagement scale for high school students. Using a quantitative descriptive design, the study involved 295 male and female students aged 15–18 years recruited through convenience sampling. The scale comprised three dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The results showed that the scale demonstrated a good model fit based on the goodness-of-fit indices (χ2/df = 1.60; CFI = 0.966; TLI = 0.962; SRMR = 0.074; RMSEA = 0.045) and good reliability, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.844 for emotional engagement, 0.753 for behavioral engagement, and 0.782 for cognitive engagement. The developed scale can be used by teachers, counselors, and educational researchers to identify students’ levels of engagement and inform the development of programs to improve student engagement.

items.title: Dialogic Co-Creation with Generative AI: Reconciling Parallel Thinking Channels, Intuition, and Epistemic Transformation in Higher Education
items.abstract: AI as a cognitive partner whose knowledge disagreements can enhance learning and intellectual development rather than merely as a technological instrument. This research paper combines theories of dialogic pedagogy, cognitive dissonance, and epistemic humility via conceptual analysis. It looks at how Parallel Thinking Channels promote critical thinking, introspection, and the innovative combination of computational reasoning with human intuition. The purpose of this study is to advance the concept of dialogic cocreation by examining the revolutionary potential of generative AI in higher education portrays. This study utilized a quantitative approach with 419 undergraduate and post-graduate students as participants. The data analysis, conceptual model and hypotheses were evaluated employing Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS version 4.1.1.8 to analyse the associations between the constructs of the study. The results of study show that the disparities arising from the conflict between machine-generated results and human reasoning serve as triggers for transformative learning. By merging intuition with computational thinking, students enhance their ability to manage uncertainty, broaden their understanding, and cultivate flexible intellectual resilience. As a cooperative partner in knowledge development, this study offers a novel framework for incorporating generative AI into higher education. To prepare graduates for complex and uncertain digital futures, it emphasizes co-creation, critical reflection, and epistemic flexibility.

items.title: Digital Innovation and Its Impact on Business Transformation in the Modern Economy
items.abstract: Abstract Digital innovation has become a major force behind the transformation of modern businesses and economies. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data analytics, the Internet of Things, blockchain, and automation has changed how organizations operate, create value, and interact with customers. Digital innovation is not limited to adopting new technologies; it also involves developing new products, services, processes, and business models. This research paper examines the concept of digital innovation and its impact on business transformation. It focuses on the major drivers of digital innovation, technologies that support it, benefits to organizations, challenges associated with implementation, and future trends. The study uses a descriptive and exploratory research methodology based primarily on secondary data collected from academic journals, books, research reports, and reliable online sources. The research finds that digital innovation can improve operational efficiency, customer experience, productivity, decision-making, and competitiveness. However, organizations face challenges such as cybersecurity threats, data privacy concerns, implementation costs, resistance to change, and a shortage of digital skills. The study concludes that organizations need appropriate strategies, skilled employees, effective leadership, and continuous innovation to successfully benefit from digital transformation.

items.title: Digital Literacy as a Predictor of AI Literacy: A Gender Paradox and a Knowledge–Belief Gap
items.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between university students’ digital literacy and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy. Participants were 770 undergraduate students (227 male, 543 female; Mage = 21.27, SD = 2.75) recruited through online convenience and snowball sampling, with recruitment centered at Karamanoğlu Mehmetbey University (Karaman, Türkiye), representing more than 120 academic programs. Data were collected with the Turkish forms of Ng’s (2012) Digital Literacy Scale (α = .931) and Wang et al.’s (2022) AI Literacy Scale (α = .803). Three findings stand out. First, digital literacy and AI literacy were strongly and positively related (r = .596, p < .001). A three-step hierarchical regression analysis identified digital literacy as the only significant predictor of AI literacy (β = .599, p < .001), explaining 35.5% of the variance (R² = .355, F(1, 768) = 422.57, p < .001); adding gender and age (ΔR² = .002) and internet use frequency (ΔR² = .000) did not significantly improve the model. Second, a small gender difference favoring men emerged in digital literacy (Cohen’s d = 0.201) but not in AI literacy (d = 0.031), a pattern we describe as a gender paradox. Third, although 85.1% of participants believed in AI’s future impact, only 22.7% rated their own AI knowledge as sufficient—a knowledge–belief gap. Self-rated AI knowledge, but not belief, differed significantly by gender (χ² = 11.05, p = .004; Cramér’s V = .120). Implications for digital and AI literacy education in higher education are discussed.

items.title: Digital Transformation and Organizational Performance: An Empirical Study of Selected Indian Organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation has emerged as an important strategic priority for organizations seeking to improve operational efficiency, innovation, customer experience and overall organizational performance. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, automation and digital platforms has significantly changed the way organizations operate and make managerial decisions. This study examines the relationship between digital transformation and organizational performance in selected Indian organizations. The study focuses on major dimensions of digital transformation, including digital technology adoption, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and automation, data analytics, digital platforms, and digital capabilities of employees. Organizational performance is examined in terms of operational efficiency, employee productivity, innovation, customer satisfaction and business performance. The study adopts a quantitative research design and proposes the collection of primary data through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation and regression analysis are proposed for testing the relationship between digital transformation and organizational performance. The study is expected to provide useful insights for managers and organizations regarding the role of digital technologies in improving organizational outcomes.

items.title: Drawbacks and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in the Medical Field
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important technology in modern healthcare. It is being used for medical image analysis, disease prediction, clinical decision support, drug discovery, patient monitoring, and administrative activities. AI can improve the speed and efficiency of healthcare, but its use also introduces significant risks. This paper examines the major drawbacks of AI in the medical field, including algorithmic bias, inaccurate predictions, lack of explainability, privacy and security risks, high implementation costs, overdependence on automated systems, accountability problems, and lack of quality training data, ethical concerns, and unequal access to AI-based healthcare. The World Health Organization (WHO) has specifically emphasized the importance of safety, transparency, human autonomy, accountability, equity, and privacy when implementing AI in healthcare. The paper also discusses possible solutions and future research directions for developing safe, reliable, and responsible medical AI.

items.title: Dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in the educational process: Assessment based on the analysis of biometric indicators under various formats of academic workload
items.abstract: Introduction. The article addresses the problem of declining cognitive engagement among students in the educational process, which negatively affects the quality of professional preparation and the formation of required competencies. Traditional methods of analysis (surveys, observation) do not allow obtaining an objective picture of the dynamics of the cognitive state during a lesson, which complicates scientifically grounded design of the educational process. The purpose of this article is to identify patterns in the dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in various formats of educational activities based on the analysis of biometric indicators. Materials and Methods. The study was conducted at the National Research Tomsk Polytechnic University during the spring semester of the 2025/2026 academic year (sample N=120). A pedagogical experiment (action research) was carried out with the participation of 120 senior students. Continuously recorded biometric parameters (heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, and skin temperature) were used as objective indicators of engagement. For integral assessment, a weighted engagement index was calculated. ANOVA, Student’s t-test, and Pearson correlation analysis were applied. Results. The authors identified statistically significant differences in students’ physiological reactions depending on the format of educational activities: practical classes cause maximum activation (index 0.78), while lectures cause minimum activation (0.42). A cyclic dynamics of attention during a 90-minute lesson was established, with a characteristic drop in concentration in the middle of the class. It was proven that the cyclic structure of the lesson prevents this dip through the alternation of work formats. It was experimentally confirmed that the introduction of the cyclic lesson structure significantly (p < 0.001) increases the integral engagement index (up to 0.76) and ensures better knowledge retention. Students in the experimental group outperformed students in the control group by 27 points when testing residual knowledge after 14-day period. Conclusions. The identified patterns in the dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in various formats of educational activities (lecture, practical class, project work) based on the analysis of biometric indicators create a scientific basis for designing classes synchronized with the natural cycles of brain performance. The proposed lesson structure facilitates the transition from passive perception of information to active cognitive activities and the formation of sustainable knowledge.

items.title: Educloud: Development of an Integrated Digital Learning Platform Based on Cloud Computing, LMS, Artificial Intelligence, and Edupreneurship
items.abstract: This study evaluated the initial feasibility and practicality of Educloud, a cloud-based digital learning platform integrating Learning Management System functions, digital assessment, learner-progress monitoring, and an AI-supported Edupreneurship workflow. Educloud was developed using Laravel and PostgreSQL, with AI functionality provided through the Google Gemini Developer API using the gemini-2.5-flash model. The AI component processes pseudonymised learner and team profiles to generate business-idea recommendations and formative feedback. The study employed a research and development approach based on an adapted ADDIE model, involving three expert validators and ten users in a small-group trial. Functional testing assessed API connectivity, contextual-data processing, privacy protection, response validation, storage, and error handling. Expert validation produced a score of 489 out of 525 (93.14%), a mean of 4.66, and an Aiken’s V of 0.91. The small-group trial produced a score of 1,117 out of 1,250 (89.36%), a mean of 4.47, and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.93. The findings indicate that Educloud demonstrates strong initial feasibility and practicality. items.title: Epistemic Situational Awareness and the Governed Knowledge Loop
items.abstract: Reasoning systems can generate claims faster than they can preserve source identity, evidentiary standing, contradiction, authority, uncertainty, and revision history. Epistemic Situational Awareness (ESA) addresses the local problem: what posture does a proposed reasoning act occupy now, and what continuations are permitted? The Governed Knowledge Loop (GKL) addresses the temporal problem: how do observations, claims, evidence, relationships, decisions, and revisions enter and evolve within a knowledge system without silently acquiring stronger standing? This paper integrates ESA and GKL as complementary capabilities of governed semantic infrastructure. ESA is defined operationally as an evidence-qualified representation of a system's epistemic position, not introspective certainty or human-like awareness. GKL is defined as a typed lifecycle whose outcomes include admission, qualification, conflict, refusal, deferral, supersession, archival, and unknown. Together they can make claim promotion and continuation more inspectable when their instrumentation, enforcement, and evidence actually cover the relevant path. The result is an architecture and evaluation program. It does not establish truth, knowledge stability, AI safety, institutional legitimacy, or a working implementation.

items.title: Ergonomics, Kaizen and Organisational Support as Pathways to Worker Well-Being in Malaysian Automotive Manufacturing: A Conceptual Framework and Research Design
items.abstract: Automotive production in Malaysia is being reshaped by automation and Industry 4.0, yet manual and semi-automated assembly work continues to expose production workers to physical strain, time pressure and the demands of continuous improvement programmes. Studies of ergonomics and Kaizen have largely developed in parallel, and the psychosocial mechanisms through which both might influence worker well-being have been rarely tested. This paper develops an integrative conceptual framework and a research design to address that gap. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, Organisational Support Theory, and Social Exchange Theory, the framework proposes that physical ergonomic factors and Kaizen practices influence worker well-being directly and indirectly, with perceived organisational support as a mediating mechanism. Five hypotheses are developed from the existing theoretical and empirical literature. A quantitative cross-sectional design is then specified for production and technical workers at automotive industry and its vendors in Tanjung Malim, Perak, covering the target population, a minimum sample of 361 respondents, a 40-item reflective measurement instrument, content and face validation, a 30-respondent pilot test and a two-step partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) analysis. This paper contributes a testable model that links technical and operational practices to Worker Well-Being through a psychosocial pathway, and it offers a replicable protocol for researchers studying production workers in comparable manufacturing settings. No empirical results are reported; the paper sets out the model and the design against which the main study will be evaluated.

items.title: Evolution of artificial intelligence in education from technology adoption to ethical governance and educator preparedness
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshapes teaching, learning, and administration, educators face pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges. This study maps the structure, themes, and research trends of AI-in-education scholarship using bibliometric and quantitative content analysis. Using the PRISMA protocol for search and screening, 208 peer-reviewed articles from the Scopus database, published between 2021 and 2025, were retrieved, and analysed using Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.5.0; R 4.6.1) and VOSviewer 1.6.21. The field is expanding rapidly, with 8 articles in 2021 and 106 in 2025 (90.79% annual growth rate). Science mapping (keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and co-citation) indicates that the field is grounded in technology-acceptance and self-efficacy theory, and features convergence around generative AI, AI literacy, and ethical application. A thematic map places educational technology and ChatGPT among motor themes and generative AI among emerging themes. A complementary content analysis of all 208 articles yields six thematic categories, the largest being students’ AI literacy, perceptions, and learning with AI tools (25.0%), AI in health-professions and other disciplinary education (21.2%), and human–AI learning frameworks (19.2%). Ethics and responsible-AI terms appear in about 40% of the articles, adoption terms in 30%, and educator-preparedness terms in 36%. The results indicate that responsible AI use is a prominent strand of the field, and give guidelines for policy, institutional leadership, faculty development and future research. The findings inform AI-in-education scholarship and educational policy aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4).

items.title: Evolution of Artificial Intelligence Models and Agents: A Survey and Future Research Directions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is all about building the systems that can observe the world carefully,think about it, learn through experience and completely the task accurately. In the last decade, progress in data, computing power and neural network architectures has produced powerful AI models, especially deep learning systems, transformers and large language models (LLMs). Building on these models, a new class of systems called AI agents can pursue goals autonomously by planning, using tools, remembering context and acting on their environment. This paper reviews the foundations of AI, the major types of AI models, the architecture and types of AI agents, their applications across sectors, and the challenges of safety, bias, privacy and governance that accompany them.

items.title: Examining Teachers’ Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence and Technostress Levels
items.abstract: Technostress refers to stress associated with the use of technology. Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to technologies that enable computer systems to perform tasks commonly associated with human intelligence. In recent years, AI has been used in many areas such as problem solving, speech processing, image recognition and image classification, and its use in education has become increasingly widespread. Against this background, the study examined teachers’ attitudes towards AI and their technostress levels. Within the scope of the research, a quantitative relational survey design was employed, and the sample consisted of 319 teachers working in schools affiliated with the Ministry of National Education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS) and the Teachers’ Techno-stress Levels Defining Scale (TTLDS). The findings revealed that teachers reported high levels of positive attitudes towards AI, moderate levels of negative attitudes, and moderate levels of technostress. The data analysis indicated a moderate positive relationship between teachers’ technostress levels and their general attitudes towards AI. In addition, teachers’ AI attitude scores differed significantly by education level and teaching branch but not by gender or age. It was also found that teachers’ scores on the technostress scale differed by gender, age and branch but not by education level.

items.title: Exploring The Use Of Generative AI In Planning, Content, And Evaluation Of Learning Among University Lecturers
items.abstract: This study examines the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) among Indonesian university lecturers across three instructional domains: learning planning, content development, and assessment. It also investigates whether AI adoption levels differ across these domains and whether adoption intensity influences usage patterns. A quantitative within-subjects design was employed, involving 306 university lecturers with prior experience using generative AI in teaching. Data were collected through a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA), following appropriate statistical assumption tests. The findings reveal relatively similar levels of AI use across the three instructional domains, with no statistically significant differences between them (p = 0.551). However, significant differences were identified between lecturers with high and low levels of AI adoption (p < 0.001), indicating consistently greater AI use among high-adoption lecturers across all domains. Furthermore, no significant interaction was found between instructional domains and adoption levels (p = 0.560). These findings suggest that the intensity of individual AI adoption plays a more prominent role in determining usage patterns than the specific instructional domain. The study highlights the importance of strengthening lecturers' AI competencies, particularly in prompt design, output verification, and ethical use, alongside institutional support to promote responsible and pedagogically meaningful AI integration in higher education.

items.title: From Automation to Educational Value: A Conceptual Framework for Human–AI Co-Learning in Education
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has increased the availability of personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, generative feedback, and automated instructional support. However, technological capability does not necessarily translate into educational value. This conceptual study addresses the question: Under what pedagogical, human, and institutional conditions does AI capability translate into educational value? A critical conceptual synthesis of research on AI-supported personalization, intelligent tutoring, generative AI, cognitive engagement, learner and teacher agency, reliability, equity, and learning authenticity was undertaken. The analysis distinguishes AI capability from educational value and identifies five dimensions through which AI-supported education can be evaluated: personalization, reliability, human agency, equity, and learning authenticity. Based on these dimensions, the study develops a Human–AI Co-Learning Framework (HACLF) comprising six interconnected layers- learner, AI assistant, teacher, learning environment, governance, and society- and proposes the AI Education Value Index (AEVI) as a conceptual evaluation framework. The conceptual synthesis indicates that the educational consequences of AI are conditional on how technological capabilities are pedagogically integrated and mediated by human judgment, verification practices, equitable access, and authentic learner participation. The study contributes an education-centred perspective that shifts evaluation from what AI can automate to the conditions under which AI can support meaningful learning. HACLF and AEVI provide a basis for future empirical research and validation of AI-supported educational practices.

items.title: From Soft-Law AI Ethics to Risk-Based Public Sector AI Procurement: Recalibrating Malaysia’s Post-PDPA Governance Model
items.abstract: Public-sector artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly acquired through procurement rather than developed entirely in-house. This shifts a central governance question from whether public institutions endorse ethical principles to whether those principles become enforceable duties across the system life cycle. Malaysia has introduced national AI governance and ethics guidance and public-sector AI adoption guidance, while the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 recalibrates parts of the data-protection framework. Yet privacy compliance and high-level ethical principles alone cannot fully govern the acquisition and operation of AI used in public administration. This article asks how Malaysia can translate soft-law principles and existing legal duties into procurement controls proportionate to risk. Using doctrinal legal analysis and functional comparison with the European Union’s AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Canada’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, it develops a normative Risk-to-Contract Accountability Framework (RCAF). The framework links risk classification to six controls: pre-award disclosure; impact assessment; contractual auditability; contestability and human review; incident reporting and material-change control; and continuing monitoring, remedies, and exit. The contribution is not a claim that AI procurement has never been studied, but a Malaysia-specific legal design connecting governance principles to the contract as a practical instrument of public accountability. The article argues that procurement should allocate responsibilities before deployment, preserve the authority’s ability to scrutinise supplier claims, and prevent contractual arrangements from insulating consequential decisions from review.

items.title: GAILC AI Liability Exposure Map (ALEM): Identifying Potential AI Liability Exposure Before Harm Occurs—An Eight-Domain Framework for Preventive Examination
items.abstract: The GAILC AI Liability Exposure Map (ALEM) is an eight-domain analytical framework developed by the Global AI Liability Consortium (GAILC) to support the preventive identification and investigation of potential AI liability exposure before harmful consequences occur. As artificial intelligence becomes integrated into consequential organizational decisions and autonomous workflows, existing governance arrangements may not fully resolve questions about decision authority, meaningful human intervention, reliance on AI-generated outputs, operational execution, evidentiary sufficiency, and responsibility across multiple actors. ALEM addresses these questions through eight interconnected exposure domains: Authority Exposure Intervention Exposure Reliance Exposure Execution Exposure Allocation Exposure Evidence Exposure Consequence and Harm Exposure Change and Autonomy Exposure The working paper establishes domain definitions, distinguishing diagnostic questions, classification boundaries, evidence requirements, and a qualitative triage procedure for prioritizing preventive examination. A constructed AI-assisted financial approval workflow demonstrates the application of all eight domains, including three illustrative triage dispositions: Immediate Examination, Priority Remediation, and Routine Monitoring. The framework draws upon established research concerning human–automation interaction, automation bias, effective oversight, and accountability. It also provides conceptual cross-references to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, and the United Kingdom Senior Managers and Certification Regime. Two practical appendices provide a preliminary assessment worksheet and a proposed assessor-consistency evaluation protocol. ALEM forms part of GAILC's Preventive AI Liability Readiness approach and connects to the GAILC Intervention Test, Allocation Test, AI System Liability Self-Check, and AI Liability Exposure Brief. The framework is presented as a foundational analytical contribution intended for practitioner application, independent examination, and future methodological refinement. Its classification reliability and predictive validity have not yet been independently established. Core principle: The map identifies conditions that warrant investigation. It does not declare that legal liability exists. items.title: GENERATIVE AI IN EFL SPEAKING AND PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CHALLENGES AND MITIGATIONS
items.abstract: While the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing instruction has received growing research attention, its impact on speaking and pronunciation remains underexplored. This PRISMA-based systematic review examines the challenges associated with using GenAI tools, particularly large language model (LLM)-based chatbots, for EFL speaking and pronunciation practice and synthesizes evidence-based mitigation strategies. Twelve studies that met the eligibility criteria yielded 48 challenges. These were organized into six thematic categories, including technical, pedagogical, learner-related, and equity concerns. The studies also varied in research design and instructional context. Several recurrent patterns emerged across the categories. Output accuracy and reliability represented the most persistent challenge and were linked to concerns about learner trust and uncritical reliance. AI-generated feedback was also repeatedly described as mechanical, formulaic, and lacking contextual sensitivity, highlighting a tension between the accessibility and scalability of these tools and limitations in areas that are important to learners. The studies commonly identified a human-in-the-loop approach as a key mitigation principle, alongside technical improvements and pedagogical interventions, including prompt literacy training. However, important questions remain unresolved, particularly whether GenAI reduces or increases teacher workload and if these tools narrow or widen existing equity gaps. Overall, the findings suggest that effective integration of GenAI into EFL speaking instruction requires attention to technical design, pedagogy, and institutional support, while several aspects of its implementation remain insufficiently understood.

items.title: Generative AI in Elementary Teacher Education: Opportunities, Risks, and Professional Ethics
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may influence how prospective elementary school teachers design, implement, and evaluate learning. It can support idea generation, lesson planning, differentiated activities, assessment rubrics, and reflective practice. However, fluent outputs are not necessarily accurate, developmentally appropriate, unbiased, or aligned with the curriculum and local sociocultural contexts. This article synthesizes the pedagogical opportunities, risks, and professional-ethical implications of GenAI use in Indonesian elementary teacher education and proposes directions for responsible integration. The study employs a narrative literature review based on exploratory searches of SciSpace, journal-publisher websites, academic sources, UNESCO publications, and Indonesian education-policy documents. The core literature covers 2020–2026, complemented by relevant foundational theory. The thematic synthesis identifies potential benefits for lesson planning and differentiation, alongside risks involving hallucinations, bias, developmental inappropriateness, privacy, copyright, unequal access, and cognitive overdependence. Responsible use requires AI literacy beyond prompt writing, including critical evaluation, ethical judgment, transparency, and accountability. The article proposes the KONTEKS framework as a guide for contextualizing, verifying, adapting, and taking responsibility for GenAI outputs. As a narrative review, it does not claim exhaustive systematic coverage or quantitative effect estimates; its recommendations require empirical testing in Indonesian elementary teacher education programs

items.title: Generative AI in Professional Learning at a Chinese Private Vocational College: Student Experiences and Teacher Perspectives
items.abstract: GenAI is now part of ordinary study for many students, but frequent use does not automatically mean deeper learning. This mixed-methods study examined professional-course use of GenAI at a private vocational college in Jiangxi Province, China. The evidence came from 431 student questionnaires and written responses from 18 teachers. After response-quality screening, 184 cases were retained for the primary quantitative analyses; 203 moderately screened cases and the full 431 responses were used for sensitivity checks. Meaningful learning engagement (MLE) was measured with two items and is therefore treated as a brief indicator of cognitive engagement rather than a validated multidimensional scale. Students reported using GenAI most often for knowledge clarification (82.6%) and coursework or exercises (74.5%); practical-training use was lower (20.7%). Perceived professional value (PPV) was associated with MLE (β = .550). When PPV and MLE were entered together, both remained associated with post-adoption learning experience (PAE; β = .339 and β = .364, respectively). The standardized indirect association from PPV to PAE through MLE was .200, with a 95% bootstrap CI of [.109, .307]. These cross-sectional results describe associations rather than causal effects. Teacher accounts added important context. Teachers valued GenAI for quick explanations but also described answer-oriented use, inaccurate professional content, weak links with practical training, and uncertainty about institutional guidance. They wanted more discipline-specific examples, clearer expectations, and assessment that made student reasoning visible. Across both strands, three tensions stood out: efficiency versus engagement, general usefulness versus professional fit, and rapid student adoption versus slower institutional response. Because the evidence came from one college, the findings should be interpreted as context-specific.
